raw_text:
**Narrative review**

Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) are foundational therapy for prevention of sudden arrhythmic death in selected secondary- and primary-prevention populations, supported by early human experience and randomized trials [1–4]. However, conventional transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs) achieve sensing, pacing, and defibrillation through endovascular leads, creating lifelong risks of venous obstruction, lead fracture, infection, perforation, and complications at generator change or system upgrade [5,6]. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed to preserve defibrillation capability while eliminating intravascular and intracardiac hardware.

The S-ICD consists of a laterally placed pulse generator and a parasternal subcutaneous electrode. It senses a far-field subcutaneous electrogram, applies rhythm discrimination algorithms, and delivers high-energy shocks; it cannot provide chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP), aside from brief post-shock pacing. Early feasibility studies established the left lateral can–parasternal coil configuration and showed reliable detection and conversion of induced ventricular fibrillation (VF) [7]. Initial single-center and national experiences confirmed implantation without fluoroscopy, high induced VF conversion rates, and the importance of patient selection and sensing-vector optimization [8,9]. A matched German case-control study similarly suggested comparable perioperative safety to TV-ICD implantation, although failed induced conversion at standard polarity and T-wave oversensing highlighted early limitations [10].

Prospective multicenter evidence rapidly expanded. The S-ICD IDE study met prespecified safety and effectiveness endpoints, with successful treatment of spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias but a notable inappropriate shock rate, largely related to oversensing [11]. The early EFFORTLESS registry showed 94% complication-free survival at 360 days and 100% overall clinical conversion after up to five shocks for discrete ventricular tachycardia/VF episodes [12]. A pooled IDE/EFFORTLESS analysis supported durable 2-year safety and efficacy [13], and midterm EFFORTLESS results in nearly 1,000 implanted patients showed low complication rates, high shock efficacy, and few conversions to TV systems for pacing [14]. Five-year EFFORTLESS follow-up demonstrated maintained first- and final-shock efficacy, no confirmed structural lead failures, and only infrequent subsequent need for pacing-capable systems [15]. The large US Post-Approval Study (PAS) broadened these observations to more heterogeneous practice settings, first reporting contemporary clinical characteristics and perioperative outcomes [16], and later showing low 5-year electrode-related complications, high final shock efficacy, and no bloodstream infections among S-ICD infections [17].

Comparative data have clarified trade-offs between S-ICD and TV-ICD therapy. Propensity-matched observational cohorts showed fewer lead-related complications with S-ICD but more pocket- or procedure-related nonlead complications, with similar inappropriate shock rates [18]. The PRAETORIAN randomized trial established noninferiority of S-ICD to TV-ICD for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks in patients with an ICD indication and no pacing requirement [19]. The ATLAS randomized trial reinforced early perioperative advantages, reporting fewer serious lead-related complications with S-ICD implantation [20]. Meta-analysis of randomized and propensity-matched studies has therefore positioned S-ICD as a valid alternative when pacing is not anticipated, particularly for younger patients, those with limited venous access, prior device infection, dialysis, congenital heart disease, or inherited arrhythmia syndromes [21].

Patient selection remains central. The ideal candidate needs defibrillation but not bradycardia pacing, CRT, or recurrent monomorphic VT likely to benefit from ATP. Primary-prevention patients with reduced ejection fraction were under-represented in early cohorts, but UNTOUCHED was designed specifically for this population [22] and reported low inappropriate shock rates using contemporary programming and discrimination algorithms [23]. Inappropriate shocks remain a key morbidity; systematic review identified oversensing, supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, programming, and device generation as determinants [24]. Infection is usually localized to the pocket or incisions and can generally be managed without the systemic consequences of endovascular infection, although complete extraction is often required [25].

Procedural technique has evolved. Intermuscular generator placement, two-incision implantation, careful parasternal tunneling, and attention to generator and coil position reduce erosion, migration, pain, and high defibrillation thresholds. The PRAETORIAN score uses posteroanterior and lateral chest radiographs to identify subcoil fat, subgenerator fat, and anterior generator position that predict failed conversion testing [26]. In the randomized PRAETORIAN-DFT trial, score-guided omission of defibrillation testing was noninferior for first-shock failure during spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias and reduced testing-related procedural risk [27]. PAS data also support the two-incision technique as safe and effective, with shorter procedure time than the original three-incision approach [28].

Current guidelines recognize S-ICD as appropriate for patients meeting ICD indications who do not require pacing, while emphasizing shared decision-making, ECG screening, and reassessment as heart failure, conduction disease, or VT substrate evolves [29,30]. Future directions include smaller devices, longer battery life, improved sensing filters, remote monitoring, and modular systems coupling S-ICD protection with leadless pacing or ATP. In contemporary practice, the S-ICD is no longer a niche device but a mature extravascular defibrillator strategy whose principal advantage—avoidance of transvenous leads—must be balanced against absent chronic pacing and the need for meticulous screening, implantation, and programming.
